reviewed: All boards together: connectors, power, signals, mechanics, bring-up
readiness: Do not order yet: 10 major system items, ASIC board has 2 blockers
headline: The boards mate pin for pin and the power and signal chains are consistent, but the system is not ready to order: the far ASIC board does not exist (SYS-05), each stack has four SPI streams for eight ASICs (SYS-04), the GT rate was sized for one ASIC instead of eight (SYS-01), and stack power, heat, ground returns, mounting, polarization, the 0.05 mm capacitor gap and ASIC rail start-up are unresolved (SYS-02, SYS-03, SYS-06 to SYS-10). Board-level problems are in the board reports; only the ASIC board has blockers (ASIC-01, ASIC-02), and the Frontend and both FPGA-LDO options carry major items. First define the far ASIC board and per-chip SPI, then recompute the GT line rate and the per-stack power and heat budget against a chosen cable.

findings.already_known: The rate is open per the FE schematic V46 note ('GT link rate/protocol ... unverified'); inputs/hdmi/design_inputs/START_HERE.md records 1.25 Gb/s as an assumption but is not flagged as wrong anywhere, and the eight-ASIC multiplier is missing there, so this is not known as an open item.
findings.title: Each cable's one GT lane must carry eight ASICs, but the only recorded line rate (1.25 Gb/s) counts one ASIC.
findings.what: Each Frontend sends all its recording data over one GT (multi-gigabit transceiver) lane, U1 TX0, through its HDMI cable. That lane must carry all eight ASICs on the Frontend: 64 data lines, 2.048 Gb/s raw or 1.536 Gb/s once the 12-bit words are packed. The only recorded line rate, about 1.25 Gb/s with an 800 ps bit, was worked out from one ASIC per port; after 8b/10b coding (a line code that sends 10 bits for every 8 data bits) it leaves only 1.0 Gb/s. A workable lane is 2.5 Gb/s (packed data) or 3.125 Gb/s (raw frames), and no line rate, framing, cable grade or loss budget has been set or checked at that rate.
findings.where: Frontend U1 (XC7A35T-2CSG325I) GTP TX0 balls H2 (P) / H1 (N); TX1-TX3 unconnected, RX balls on GND. J3 pin 5 = GTP_TX0_P, pin 3 = GTP_TX0_N (swap intended, TXPOLARITY=1). Micro-HDMI cable, about 1.8 m. HDMI Extension Board J610-J617 pins 3/5 -> ESD U801-U808 -> AC capacitors C745-C760 -> MC3 GTY RX quads 224/226 (rec_rx[0..7]).
findings.evidence: inputs/hdmi/design_inputs/START_HERE.md line 17: 256 Mbit/s per port, about 1.25 Gb/s (assumed), 800 ps; line 34: skew and spacing items to be reopened if the rates are higher; line 36: cable about 1.8 m. inputs/hdmi/power_estimate/START_HERE.md line 31: one GTP TX lane at about 1.25 Gb/s (its line 28 lists 64 DATA lines). inputs/frontend/V2_review_fixes/Frontend_V46_pins_V2.xdc and exports/frontend/nets.csv: 64 nets ASIC1-8_DATA1-8, J1/J2 to U1. ASIC_REFERENCE.md section 3, line 51: 256 Mbit/s raw, 192 Mbit/s payload per ASIC; x 8 = 2.048 Gb/s raw, 1.536 Gb/s payload. Reference clocks are 125 MHz on both ends (Frontend Y1 AX3DAF1-125.0000T3; the XEM's on-module oscillator for rec_refclk). With UG482 dividers the reachable lane rates are 1.875, 2.0, 2.5, 3.125 and 3.75 Gb/s. 8b/10b payload: 1.25 -> 1.0 Gb/s (too low); 2.0 -> 1.6 Gb/s (96 % load with packed data, too tight); 2.5 -> 2.0 Gb/s (77 % packed); 3.125 -> 2.5 Gb/s (82 % raw). Nyquist frequency rises from 0.625 GHz to 1.25-1.56 GHz. The Frontend schematic note lists 'GT link rate/protocol, cable SI' as unverified; no later lane-rate decision was found in inputs/ or the 3-11 Nov dated folders.
findings.source: ASIC reference V1 (inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/ASIC_REFERENCE.md) section 3, line 51; AMD DS181 v1.27.1 Table 52 (GTP maximum 6.25 Gb/s for -2 in CS/CP packages; PLL range 1.6-3.3 GHz; line rate 3.2-6.6 Gb/s at output divider 1), https://www.amd.com/content/dam/xilinx/support/documents/data_sheets/ds181_Artix_7_Data_Sheet.pdf; AMD UG482 7 Series GTP Transceivers, PLL dividers; engineering judgement. The HDMI cable-category limit was quoted from memory and not re-read.
findings.consequence: If cables or firmware are planned around 1.25 Gb/s, the link cannot carry eight ASICs. At 2.5-3.125 Gb/s a thin 1.8 m Micro-HDMI cable with its ESD parts and connectors may not give an open eye, which shows up as bit errors and lost recording frames on some ports.
findings.suggested_action: Record the lane rate and framing (2.5 Gb/s with packed 12-bit data, or 3.125 Gb/s with raw frames) and reopen the HDMI-board items tied to the rate. Run an IBERT eye and loss check over one real cable at 1.25-1.56 GHz Nyquist before buying eight sets.

findings.already_known: inputs/hdmi/power_estimate/START_HERE.md gate 3 / gates A2-A3 ('Check pin-19 resistance and current capability', XPE) and inputs/hdmi/V35_prefab_review/ALL_FINDINGS.md (cable drop, should-fix) are still open. Both reviewers agree it is open; the constant-power effect and the added LDO/ASIC load make it more urgent than the 0.55 A figure suggests, since the high-case stack meets the port limit even before cable loss.
findings.title: High-load stacks reach the 637 mA port current limit on a 1.8 m cable with 30-32 AWG or thinner +5 V wire.
findings.what: Each stack (Frontend, FPGA-LDO board and four ASIC boards) gets all its power through pin 19 of its Micro-HDMI cable, a single +5 V wire. The Frontend buck U16 draws close to constant power, so when the cable voltage drops its current rises. With a perfect cable the high-load case needs about 0.55-0.58 A, below the port switch's 637 mA minimum limit, but once the cable loop resistance passes about 0.9-1.3 ohm (30-32 AWG at 1.8 m) it reaches that limit, and at 34-36 AWG there is no usable operating point. The expected load works on every gauge; the Frontend power has never been estimated with Vivado/XPE and the chosen cable's wire gauge is unknown, so a power estimate and a measured cable loop resistance are needed.
findings.where: HDMI Extension Board U701-U708 (TPS2553DBVR, R711-R718 37.4k) OUT -> PORT1_5V..PORT8_5V -> J610-J617 pin 19; cable +5 V wire; Frontend J3.19 -> VIN_5V -> U16 MPM3833C (IN 13/14, EN 4) -> VIN_3V3 -> every Frontend regulator and J2.68-70 to the FPGA-LDO board (its only supply input). Return on pins 4/7/10/13/16 and the shell.
findings.evidence: TPS2553 limit with 37.4k (eq. 1-3): 636.6 / 696.0 / 763.6 mA min/typ/max (about 630 mA min with a 1 % resistor); rDS(on) DBV 85 mOhm typ, 135 mOhm max over temperature. Load: inputs/hdmi/power_estimate/START_HERE.md section 1 gives 1.2 W / 2.4 W at VIN_3V3, which already include 0.13 / 0.30 A for the LDO/ASIC boards (0.30 A is the DF40 contact rating, not an estimate); scratch/system-power/budget.py gives 1.45 W expected and 2.79 W high at 5 V, about 5 % above the record. Perfect cable, high case: 0.55-0.58 A. Re-run models at 1.8 m (scratch/system-mate-cable/cable_power.py, scratch/system-power/cable.py, scratch/verify-system-f2-files/cable_check.py), high case: 28 AWG 575-625 mA; 30 AWG 594-654 mA; 32 AWG 631-716 mA; 34 AWG 0.72-0.95 A (past the minimum and typical limits) or no solution; 36 AWG no solution. Loop resistance at which the high case reaches 637 mA: 0.90-1.32 Ohm. Expected case at 36 AWG: 362-394 mA, 3.7-4.0 V at U16, which needs about 3.41 V; a 36 AWG loop delivers at most about 1.9 W, about 30 % over the expected load. The high case is a pessimistic envelope (VCCINT 0.4 A, every stimulator at full current).
findings.source: TI TPS2553 datasheet SLVS841G (rev. Oct 2026), sec. 6.5 p.6-7 and sec. 8.5.1 eq. 1-3 p.16-17, https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/tps2553.pdf; MPS MPM3833C Rev 1.0, p.4 (UVLO 2.3-2.75 V rising, 400 mV hysteresis, dropout resistance 130 mOhm), https://www.monolithicpower.com/en/mpm3833c.html; copper resistance per AWG from standard tables; engineering judgement. The 0.8 A connector contact rating comes from distributor data and was not checked against the Molex datasheet.
findings.consequence: In the high case the port switch goes into current limit or cycles, VIN_5V falls toward U16's undervoltage lockout, and the Frontend and the LDO/ASIC rails brown out or reset. Slim cables, which the 9.86 mm port pitch pushes toward, make this more likely.
findings.suggested_action: Get a Vivado report_power or XPE estimate for the Frontend and measure the pin-19 plus return loop resistance of the chosen cable; accept only cables below about 0.9 Ohm loop. If the high case is real, cut the stack load rather than raise the limit (30.1k gives 794 mA min but 936 mA max, above the 0.8 A contact rating).

findings.title: No record estimates or limits head-stack heat; about 1.45 W per stack gives a 19-34 K still-air surface rise.
findings.what: Nearly all power that enters a stack becomes heat in it: the FPGA, the 5 V-to-3.3 V buck and the other bucks, the linear regulators and the ASIC boost converter. The Option A stack is small (24.12 x 47.05 x 13.82 mm), so in still air its average surface rises about 19-34 K at the expected 1.45 W, with hot spots over U1 and the bucks running higher. Eight stacks stand side by side on the animal's skull with probe shanks in the brain, so they heat each other and the head, about 11.6 W in total at the expected load. No record sets a temperature limit, and only a measurement of one powered stack running the real bitstream will give the real rise.
findings.where: Frontend U1 (XC7A35T), U16 and U2/U3/U4/U13 (MPM3833C), U5/U6 (TPS74801), U10 (MP5077); FPGA-LDO A U1 (LT3582-12), U2/U6/U8/U9 (LT3042), U10 (LT3094), U3/U4/U5/U7 (TPS7A2015); four ASIC boards per stack; whole Option A stack (Option B is larger and similar).
findings.evidence: scratch/system-power/budget.py: 1.45 W expected, 2.79 W high at VIN_5V; rail currents match inputs/hdmi/power_estimate/START_HERE.md section 1 and inputs/asic/J3_pinout__Power_Budget.csv. A low case of about 1.1 W follows from the record's low column plus the boost. Envelope 24.12 x 47.05 x 13.82 mm (inputs/system/README_2026-11-11.md; matches Option_A_Head_Stack_V12.stl without the plug) -> 4,237 mm2. h = 10-15 W/m2K -> 15.7-23.6 K/W -> 23-34 K at 1.45 W, 17-26 K at 1.1 W, 44-66 K at 2.8 W. A convection plus radiation estimate gives h about 13-16 W/m2K, so about 19-23 K expected. The 2.8 W case assumes all 1,024 stimulators at 22.5 uA on both rails continuously and VCCINT 0.4 A; with 1 ms pulses under 200 Hz and one rail per phase it falls to about 2.1 W (about 33 K). Option B (27.90 x 52.88 x 13.77 mm, 5,175 mm2) rises about 20 % less. Eight stacks: 9-22 W, 11.6 W expected. inputs/system/weekly_deck/START_HERE.md (11 Nov 08:24 entry): eight stacks on a sheep skull, shanks in the brain. A search of inputs/ found no head-stack thermal estimate or limit.
findings.source: Engineering judgement (lumped surface model). The IEC 60601-1 applied-part surface limit of about 43 C for long contact is from secondary sources and was not read; tissue-heating limits (usually about 1-2 K brain temperature rise) are stricter. Efficiency curves of the LT3582-12, MPM3833C and TPS74801 were not checked against the datasheets.
findings.consequence: Stack surfaces above body-contact limits, heat conducted down the shanks into the brain, and hot FPGA and ASIC junctions; the planned commercial-grade U1 (XC7A35T-2CSG325C, 0-85 C) leaves less junction margin. This may force a heat sink, duty cycling or a head-mount change after eight stacks are built.
findings.suggested_action: Set a head-surface and tissue-heating limit, then measure one powered stack (thermocouple or IR) in still air with the real bitstream before ordering eight.

findings.already_known: inputs/notes/fpga-ldo-v14.md (6 Nov: far board shares CLKH/SPI_CLK/SPI_DIN) records sharing as accepted, without addressing the designer's 'Not Shared' grouping; inputs/asic/sandwich_hub_options/START_HERE.md lists as open whether the far board gets BOARD2/BOARD4 clocks and separate SPI pins, and Frontend V46 has since dropped those lines. findings.title: Each stack has four stimulation SPI data pairs for eight ASICs, so paired near and far chips get one stream.
findings.what: Each ASIC has its own SPI_DL and SPI_DR inputs (the serial lines that load its configuration and stimulation tables), and the ASIC designer's pin sheet lists them under 'Not Shared'. The Frontend brings out only four pairs (STIM_CHIP1..4_SPI_DL/DR), and the ASIC board passes SPI_DINR/SPI_DINL straight from J3 to J4 with no T_ copy, so the far board's chip in each position receives the near chip's stream. With SPI_CLK and SPI_LATCH also shared and no chip address in the stream, each pair gets the same gain, DAC settings and stimulation table, and a far chip cannot be left idle. The sheet groups the pins but does not forbid sharing, so this is a decision for the ASIC designer and the board's owner; if a far-board variant instead moved SPI to the spare pins 2/4/6/8/24/58, those pins are open on both FPGA-LDO designs and the far chips would get no SPI at all.
findings.where: Frontend U1 C11/G14 (CHIP1), C14/C16 (CHIP2), V7/V6 (CHIP3), N17/N18 (CHIP4). FPGA-LDO A and Option B router: J4 pins 57/59 (STIM_CHIP1) and 23/25 (CHIP2), J3 pins 57/59 (CHIP3) and 23/25 (CHIP4); J3/J4 pins 2, 4, 6, 8, 24, 58 open. ASIC board J3 = J4 on SPI_DINR 57, SPI_DINL 59, SPI_DINR(2) 23, SPI_DINL(2) 25. Pairs: CHIP1 -> ASIC1 + ASIC3, CHIP2 -> ASIC2 + ASIC4, CHIP3 -> ASIC5 + ASIC7, CHIP4 -> ASIC6 + ASIC8.

findings.suggested_action: Ask the ASIC designer whether paired chips may share one SPI stream. If not, route eight more SPI data lines (four per ASIC port) over the spare connector pins on the Frontend and the FPGA-LDO before ordering either.

findings.title: No CAD exists for the far ASIC board that must drive the T_ lanes, so half the J3/J4 pin map is unchecked.
findings.what: The only ASIC-board CAD in the workspace (from the folder named 'Bottom') passes 74 of its 80 J3 pins straight to the same J4 pin; its two chips drive the odd-numbered lanes (D<1..8>, READ, SYNC, CLK32MHZ, DISC_OUT), and the 22 T_ ('through') nets touch only the connectors. FPGA-LDO A and the Option B router read ASIC3/4/7/8 from those T_ pins, so they rely on a far-board variant whose chips drive the T_ pins instead, and no such file exists in any copy in the workspace. If four copies of the existing board were stacked, each pair would tie two chip outputs together on 22 lanes and on DISC_OUT pins 3 and 5, and leave 22 lanes undriven. The project record says a top board is ready, so the files cannot settle this; the far board's KiCad file from the ASIC designer would.
findings.where: ASIC board J3/J4 (all 80 pins), U01_BCD1/U01_BCD2; T_ pins 10-22, 26-32 and 60-80 even; DISC_OUT pins 3/5; spare pins 2/4/6/8/24/58. findings.title: Option B J5 carries 108 signals with only three return contacts: GND on pins 3 and 65 and AGND on pin 62.
findings.what: J5, the 120-pin DF40 board-to-board connector between the Option B router and LDO board, uses every contact: 108 single-ended 1.5 V signals, 9 ASIC rails and only three returns. A fast signal's return current flows back along the nearest ground path, and 51 of the 108 signals are more than 5 mm from a GND contact, so about 80 lines switching together at 32 MHz can cause crosstalk and ground bounce. The AGND planes on both boards also act as reference planes for signal layers, and AGND joins GND at NT1 about 6.6 mm from J5, so pin 62 carries switching digital return current as well as the analog return of eight ASICs; that mixing is the main analog risk, while the DC drop (about 1-4.4 mV) is negligible. ASIC output edge rates are not documented, so the files cannot show whether three returns are enough; a decision on more returns, or measured edge rates, would settle it.
findings.where: Option B router J5 (DF40C-120DS) and LDO board J5 (DF40C-120DP): GND pins 3 and 65, AGND pin 62; the four MP pads on the LDO-board header have no net. findings.title: No head board has a fixing feature, so the stack and the HDMI cable load hang on unlocked DF40 connectors.
findings.what: None of the five head boards (Frontend, FPGA-LDO Option A, Option B router, Option B LDO board, ASIC board) has a mounting hole, slot, notch or standoff. The 70-, 80- and 120-position DF40 parts used here have no latch, and Hirose says a board must not be held by these connectors alone but secured with a housing or cushioning. The Micro-HDMI cable plugs into the Frontend, so every plug-in, pull-out, tug or twist of the cable is carried by the 140 contacts of Frontend J1/J2, which engage by only 0.45 mm. No record says how the stack is held on the animal or where the cable is anchored; the weekly deck says the head cap is not drawn.
findings.where: All five head boards. Frontend J1/J2 (DF40C-70DS-0.4V(51), bottom) on FPGA-LDO J1/J2 (DF40C-70DP-0.4V(51)) of Option A and of the Option B LDO board; Frontend J3 Micro-HDMI (Molex 467651001) at (112.5, 98.28), top, plug entering from the north edge; LDO A J3/J4, router J3/J4 and J5, ASIC board J3/J4.

findings.title: Unkeyed DF40 pairs let an ASIC board mate rotated 180 degrees, putting +/-10 V onto ASIC clock and data pins.
findings.what: Hirose states the DF40 connector is not polarized, and no head board has a key, hole, standoff or an orientation mark that stays visible after mating (the Frontend has no silkscreen; the LDO and ASIC boards have only pin-1 triangles, hidden under the mated connector). A rotated Frontend cannot mate in a full stack, because its bottom parts sit over the LDO J3 (Option B: J5) header and it overlaps the ASIC board or router in the same 1.5 mm plane, so it rests at least 1.6 mm high and its contacts never touch. A partly built stack (a Frontend fitted before the J3 ASIC board, or the Option B LDO board without its router) is also exposed.

findings.title: The FPGA cannot switch or monitor the ASIC rails or +/-12 V converter; they are on whenever the cable is live.
findings.what: On the FPGA-LDO boards the shared enable for all nine ASIC regulators and the LT3582 +/-12 V converter is only a resistor and capacitor from VIN_3V3, and VIN_3V3 itself is always on once the cable is powered. No enable signal comes from the FPGA and no power-good (a regulator's 'output is in range' signal) goes back, so the FPGA cannot hold off, sequence, watch or shut down the ASIC supplies, and swapping an ASIC board means pulling the cable or hot-plugging. The back-powering at start-up claimed in the original does not happen: the ASIC rails rise about 15-22 ms after VIN_3V3, well after the FPGA's 1.5 V I/O bank (about 3 ms), while the FPGA pins are still undriven. Power-down order is not settled by the files and needs a scope capture; the open point is whether the ASIC designer's still-unknown sequencing and pin limits require FPGA control, which is cheap to add only before ordering.

findings.consequence: The FPGA cannot sequence the ASICs, keep them off during FPGA bring-up, shut down the +/-12 V converter or react to a failed rail. findings.suggested_action: Get the ASIC power-up and power-down order and powered-off pin limits from the ASIC designer, and decide before ordering whether the FPGA gates the rails; if so, route a Frontend-driven enable on a spare pin (for example J1.29) to EN_ASIC_RAILS with R1 as a pull-down and return a wired-OR power-good. If not, write 'cable unplugged before any DF40 is mated or unmated' into the bring-up procedure and capture the power-down order on a scope.

findings.title: No record sets a grounding rule for eight stacks on one animal, each tied to base ground by its own cable.
findings.what: On every stack the ASIC analogue ground (AGND, which also carries the ASIC board's one-pin ground pin J1) joins digital ground at the net tie NT1, and that ground runs through the cable shell and ground pins to the HDMI Extension Board ground and on to the PC. All stacks meet at that one point, which is the normal arrangement for multi-headstage recording rigs, so there is no ground loop unless stacks are also joined at the head end, for example through separate ground electrodes in the same animal, a shared frame or another earthed instrument. Each stack's 0.15-0.55 A supply return flows in its own cable, so each stack's ground sits roughly 15-190 mV from the base board ground; the differences between stacks are probably smaller but are not known. No record says how the eight stacks on one animal are to be grounded.

findings.consequence: If stacks on one animal are given separate ground electrodes, the stack-to-stack offsets drive current through tissue and show up as hum, offset and common-mode noise, with possible electrode corrosion. findings.suggested_action: Write a rig grounding rule: one common ground electrode (for example a skull screw) for all stacks on an animal, never separate grounds. With the first two powered stacks, measure the stack-to-stack ground offset, hum, and the current in the shared ground wire and ASIC J1.

findings.title: Eight stacks need PCIe Gen3 x4 to the host, but no record states Gen3 or packed samples as a requirement.
findings.what: Eight stacks of eight ASICs produce 12.3 Gb/s (1.54 GB/s) of packed 12-bit samples, or 16.4 Gb/s (2.05 GB/s) if each sample is sent as a 16-bit word, before framing. The only host path that can carry this is the HDMI Extension Board's PCIe x4 link; at Gen2 it cannot carry 16-bit words and has almost no margin for packed data, while Gen3 carries either, and the XEM8310 USB 3 interface is several times too slow. Every part of the chain already supports Gen3 x4 (the FPGA's PCIe block, the Thunderbolt adapter and the board layout), so the open generation is a firmware IP setting plus a bring-up test, not a copper change. The project record states the system rate (about 2 GB/s) but does not tie it to the host-link generation or record a fallback.

findings.title: Each stacked ASIC board's J1 pin tail lands on the J1 below and holds two DF40 joints about 0.24 mm open.
findings.what: J1 on the ASIC board is a single 1.00 mm right-angle pin on AGND whose tail goes through the board. All four ASIC boards put J1 at the same x/y, so in KiCad's generic 3D model each upper board's tail comes down onto the bent lead of the J1 below. That holds the DF40 board-to-board joint between those two boards about 0.24 mm short of fully mated, about half of its 0.45 mm effective mating length (the travel over which the contacts touch). Both pins are AGND, so this is a seating problem, not a short; the pin has no part number, so the real tail length is unknown and only the chosen pin's drawing can settle the true overlap.

findings.title: The +10 V and -10 V connector pins sit 0.4 mm from 1.5 V rail pins, and on LDO B J5 beside an ASIC data line.
findings.what: On every 80-pin DF40 connector J3/J4, the +10 V pin (VDD10) and the -10 V pin (VSS10) each have a 1.5 V rail pin on both sides, 0.4 mm apart. A solder bridge between neighbours would put 8.5 V or 11.5 V on 1.5 V rails shared by all eight ASICs on a head and on regulator outputs rated far below that. This pin order comes from the ASIC designer's pin table and is fixed by the ASIC board; nothing fails as drawn, so it is a bring-up and assembly hazard. The not-yet-ordered LDO B J5 repeats the pattern and puts VSS10 next to ASIC1_DATA4, which runs straight to an FPGA pin.

findings.title: An open or wrong SET resistor drives an ASIC rail to about 3.2 V or +/-11.7 V, and nothing clamps it.
findings.what: The LT3042 and LT3094 regulators set their output as 100 uA times one SET resistor to AGND. If that 0402 resistor is open or the wrong value, the output ramps toward the input minus dropout, and every rail goes to all eight ASICs on a head with no clamp. The unused power-good (PG) pins are left the way the data sheet allows, and PG only flags a low output, so wiring it would not catch this fault; the inherited LDO Board A had the same exposure on nine rails. The ASIC's absolute voltage limits are not known, so the files cannot say whether this damages the ASICs; only limits from the ASIC designer would settle it.

findings.title: On ports 1, 2, 7 and 8 the Frontend's dedicated SYNC input floats, and the Frontend cannot tell its port.

findings.title: The Frontend cable connector has no ESD protection on the GT pair, JTAG pins, sense pin or 5 V input.
findings.what: The head end of the cable is the one plugged and unplugged most, so it is where a static discharge from the cable is most likely. On the Frontend only the clock, command and SYNC LVDS pairs pass through an ESD array (U17, U18 TPD4E02B04). The transceiver (GT) transmit pair, the four JTAG lines, the sense line and the 5 V input go to the FPGA or the power input with no protection part. The HDMI Extension Board's ESD parts protect only that board, and on it the JTAG and sense lines pass only through 100 ohm resistors and an analog switch.

findings.title: The XEM can drive LVDS pairs into an unpowered Frontend, back-feeding its 1.5 V bank through clamp diodes.
findings.what: The XEM drives the clock, command and SYNC pairs on every port whenever its bitstream runs, but it cannot tell whether a port's Frontend is powered. On a live plug, or when a port is in fault or current limit, the Frontend's VCCO_1V5 rail is at or near 0 V, so up to 4 LVDS legs (6 on ports 3-6) push current through the Artix-7 clamp diodes (protection diodes from each pin to its bank supply) and can partly lift the dead rail. This does not happen on a normal cold start, because the ports power up about 10 ms after 12 V, before the XEM is configured. The files cannot settle how much current flows; the LVDS driver current is expected to stay below the 10 mA clamp limit, and a measurement of VCCO_1V5 during a live plug would settle it.

findings.title: Frontend JTAG uses HDMI pin 2 for TMS, a wire that cables without Ethernet may leave out.
findings.what: The Frontend's JTAG runs as single wires in the roughly 1.8 m HDMI cable: TMS on pin 2 (Utility/HEAC+), TDI on 15 (CEC), TCK on 17 (SCL) and TDO on 18 (SDA). Pin 2 is only sure to be wired in 'with Ethernet' cables. Cable JTAG is the Frontend's only JTAG path, so a cable without pin 2 means the Frontend cannot be configured and its flash cannot be programmed. Crosstalk from TCK onto TDO is plausible but the files cannot settle it: neighbouring connector pins do not show how the wires lie inside a given cable, and only the cable's construction or a measurement would.

findings.consequence: A cable that lacks the pin-2 wire leaves that Frontend unprogrammable; TDO errors at high TCK are possible but unproven.

findings.title: Paste openings on every DF40 land pattern equal the pad, where Hirose recommends an 80 % opening.

Hirose recommends a 0.12 mm stencil with an 80 % opening on both the receptacle (DS) and header (DP) halves, and warns that excess solder and flux can wick into the contacts. No pad, footprint or board paste margin or ratio is set anywhere, and the order notes give no stencil instruction.

findings.title: DF40 joints are rated for 30 mating cycles, and no record says how often each stack will be unplugged.
findings.what: Hirose rates every DF40 for 30 mate/unmate cycles, with contact resistance at most 90 mOhm after them; nothing is specified beyond 30. The removable joints are the Frontend on the LDO A in Option A and the plug-in LDO board on the router in Option B, and the half that stays on the head wears with every swap. Several records state the 30-cycle rating, but none says how many unplugs are expected or keeps a mate count. This is a usage decision, not a board defect.

findings.title: Each J3/J4 joint has only four ground contacts, all near the middle, for about 60 signals.
findings.what: The inherited ASIC pinout puts AGND on pins 42/44 and GND/DGND on 46/48 and nothing else, so signals near the connector ends are up to 7-8 mm from a return path (the ground contact that carries each signal's return current back). On the FPGA-LDO side 21 (J3) and 23 (J4) of 60 used signals are more than 5 mm from a ground. The files cannot show whether this causes crosstalk; that depends on the ASIC output edge rate and needs a measurement at bring-up. The FPGA-LDO cannot add grounds here without the ASIC designer's agreement.

findings.title: Ten ASIC-board pass-through vias are open holes inside or at the edge of DF40 pads, so solder can wick away.
findings.what: Five far-board pass-through lanes have no track: each reaches the bottom J3 pad only through one via whose copper ring overlaps the pad by 0.045 mm. That join is one copper shape about 0.19 mm wide on the same layer, so it is connected, but the drilled hole sits only 0.005 mm from the pad edge. On the top side the holes of these five vias lie fully inside J4 header pads, and five more vias have 0.105 mm of their hole inside a J4 pad. Unless the vias are filled and capped (plugged and plated over), solder can drain down these open holes (via-in-pad) and weaken the 0.4 mm-pitch joints.
findings.evidence: pcbnew on boards/asic/PCB.kicad_pcb: the five (2) nets have 0 tracks, length 0.00, one through via each (drill 0.15 mm, land 0.25 mm), no zone. J3 DS pad 0.20 x 0.70 at y 69.47 (y 69.12-69.82); J4 DP pad 0.23 x 0.66 at y 69.65 (y 69.32-69.98). Overlap h = 0.045 mm with r = 0.125 mm: area about 0.006 mm2, chord about 0.19 mm. The other five nets have vias at y 69.950 plus 0.48 mm of track; the remaining T_ nets have vias at y 70.40, outside the pads. exports/asic/drc.json: 0 unconnected items.

findings.consequence: Starved or weak solder joints on far-board lanes after assembly, which KiCad DRC does not flag.
findings.suggested_action: Ask the ASIC designer to order filled and capped vias, or to move these vias off the pads and add short tracks.

findings.title: Each stack's power crosses one Micro-HDMI contact and one cable wire of unrecorded gauge, with little margin.
findings.what: Each stack gets all its power through one contact, Micro-HDMI pin 19, and one wire in the cable. The Molex receptacle contact is listed at 0.8 A at 25 C; the project estimates 0.27 A expected and 0.55 A high per port, and a constant-power load (regulators that draw more current as their input voltage falls) can reach about 0.65 A on a thin 1 m cable, 81 % of the rating. The port switch passes its full 764 mA only while it is limiting current, which is a fault state. The gauge of the cable's +5 V wire is not recorded, so the files cannot settle the wire and contact heating; naming the cable and measuring loop resistance and temperature at full load would.
findings.where: HDMI Extension Board J610-J617 pin 19 (Molex 467651001, nets PORTn_5V); Frontend J3 pin 19 (net VIN_5V); the cable's +5 V conductor. No other pin carries 5 V (pins 4/7/10/13/16 and the shell are DGND).
findings.evidence: exports/hdmi/connectors.csv and exports/frontend/connectors.csv: pin 19 is the only power pin. exports/hdmi/parts.csv: U701-U708 TPS2553DBVR with R711-R718 37.4k, giving current limits of 637/696/764 mA (min/typ/max, SLVS841G eq. 1-3, p.16-17). inputs/hdmi/power_estimate/START_HERE.md: 0.15/0.27/0.55 A at the 5 V pin. Contact load at the estimates: 34-81 % of 0.8 A (0.65 A case from the V35 cable-drop analysis). Wire heating at 0.55 A: about 0.26 W/m for 34 AWG to 0.41 W/m for 36 AWG. inputs/hdmi/V35_prefab_review/ALL_FINDINGS.md lines 209, 231 and 316-320 already record the 0.8 A rating, the 34 AWG assumption, the 0.65 A at 1 m case and a should-fix cable-drop item.
findings.source: Molex 46765-1001 listing, 0.8 A per contact at 25 C, https://www.molex.com/en-us/products/part-detail/467651001 (page timed out; value from Molex and distributor summaries; Molex specification PS-46765 not read). TI TPS2553 datasheet SLVS841G, eq. 1-3, p.16-17, https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/tps2553.pdf.
findings.consequence: The contact and cable run warm at high load in a head-mounted, warm setting; contact wear over mating cycles raises resistance and adds to the known cable-drop problem.
findings.suggested_action: Name the cable, including the gauge of its +5 V wire, in the build record, and measure pin-19-to-ground loop resistance and cable temperature at full load (about 0.65 A) before ordering eight.

findings.already_known: V35 prefab review notes U16 has no UVLO divider (inputs/hdmi/V35_prefab_review/ALL_FINDINGS.md).
findings.title: A port in current limit leaves the Frontend browned out, not shut down, and the XEM cannot see the fault.
findings.what: Frontend buck module U16 (MPM3833C) has its enable pin tied straight to VIN_5V, so it keeps running down to its own input lockout of 2.3-2.75 V. If a port's TPS2553 switch limits current, VIN_5V sags and U16 can sit in dropout (input too low to regulate) with VIN_3V3 partly up, while the TPS2553 stays in current limit and cycles on its 135 C thermal shutdown. Each FAULT output drives only an LED, so the XEM8310 cannot see or clear a port fault. A resistor divider on U16 EN would not fix this: EN is a logic input (on above 1.2 V, off only below 0.3 V, internal 1 MOhm pull-down), not a precise threshold.
findings.where: Frontend: U16 pin 4 EN (and pins 13/14) on VIN_5V; U16 pin 12 PG unconnected. HDMI Extension Board: U701-U708 pin 4 FAULT to D701-D708 cathodes only; PORT_ENABLE driven only by U700 PG; R711-R718 37.4k.
findings.evidence: exports/frontend/netlist.xml: VIN_5V (8 nodes) = J3.19, U16.4/13/14, C206/C207/C209, TP14; U16.12 PG unconnected. exports/hdmi/netlist.xml: each Net-(D70x-K) has 2 nodes (U70x.4 FAULT and the LED cathode); PORT_ENABLE has 10 nodes (U700.13 PG, R703, eight EN pins), no XEM pin. MPM3833C Rev 1.0 p.4: UVLO rising 2.3/2.5/2.75 V, 400 mV hysteresis, EN logic low 0.3 V, logic high 1.2 V; p.12: internal 1 MOhm EN pull-down. TPS2553 with 37.4k: limit 637-764 mA; constant-current limiting and thermal turn-off at 135 C minimum while in current limit (sec. 8.3.1, 8.3.6). inputs/hdmi/V35_prefab_review/ALL_FINDINGS.md lines 192-194 and 328-335 already record that FAULT is not seen by the XEM, the cable-drop collapse and EN tied to VIN_5V.
findings.source: MPS MPM3833C datasheet Rev 1.0, p.4 (UVLO, EN thresholds) and p.12 (Enable), https://www.monolithicpower.com/en/mpm3833c.html; TI TPS2553 datasheet SLVS841G, sec. 8.3.1, 8.3.3 and 8.3.6, https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/tps2553.pdf.
findings.consequence: Partial-power states on the FPGA and ASIC rails, repeated TPS2553 thermal cycling, and data loss that firmware cannot diagnose.
findings.suggested_action: On the next Frontend spin, put a supervisor or a load switch with a precise UVLO ahead of U16 (not an EN divider), or record that the existing U12/PG reset chain is accepted; on any HDMI board spin, route the eight FAULT outputs (or a wired-OR) to an XEM input.

findings.title: Driving Frontend pin M15 low to switch off the GT rails instead resets and reloads the FPGA, in a loop.
findings.what: FPGA pin M15 drives EN_GTPWR_1V5, which through U15 enables buck U13; U13's power-good (PG, a pin that goes low when a regulator is off or out of regulation) is the only enable of U5, the transceiver supply regulator. U5's PG is tied with U4's into BOOT_RAILS_PG_3V3, the manual-reset input of reset chip U12, which then pulls PROGRAM_B and INIT_B low through U11 and erases the FPGA's configuration. With the FPGA blank, M15 floats, R58 pulls the enable high, the rails return and the FPGA reloads, so any design that drives M15 low repeats this about every 7 s. The 'shutdown function' promised in the U15 field cannot be used.
findings.where: Frontend: U1 M15 (EN_GTPWR_1V5), R58 4.99k to VCCO_1V5, U15, EN_GTPWR_3V3 (U13.4, R57), PG_GTP_1V4 (U13.12, U5.5, R43), BOOT_RAILS_PG_3V3 (R9, TP10, U4.12, U5.3, U6.5, U12.3 MR), BOOT_RESET_N (U12.6 to U11.1/U11.3, U14.2), FPGA_PROGRAM_B (U11.6 to U1 P10), FPGA_INIT_B (U11.4 to U1 T10), C84 1 uF on U12 CT, R25 PUDC_B to VCCO_1V5.
findings.evidence: exports/frontend/netlist.xml: the nets listed under where. TPS748 SBVS074N sec. 6.3.2, p.17: PG goes low when the device is disabled or VOUT falls below about 90 %. TPS3890 SLVSD65A p.3: MR low asserts RESET, which stays low for the delay after MR returns high; tPD = 1.07 s per uF, so about 1.07 s with C84 (more than the '>=215 ms' in the U12 field). U7 field: 17,536,096 bits at 3 MHz SPI x1 = 5.85 s. Cycle about 7 s. PUDC_B strapped high (R25), so M15 has no configuration pull-up. inputs/frontend/V2_review_fixes/Frontend_V46_pins_V2.xdc lines 118-119: M15 constrained LVCMOS15 as an FPGA output.
findings.source: TI TPS748 datasheet SBVS074N (June 2024), sec. 6.3.2, p.17; TI TPS3890 datasheet SLVSD65A, p.3 (pin functions, CT formula) and p.4; MPS MPM3833C Rev 1.0, p.4 (PG, soft-stop). Engineering judgement on the drawn netlist.
findings.consequence: A firmware default of 0 on M15, or a power-saving feature, puts the Frontend into an endless reconfiguration loop of about 7 s per cycle.
findings.suggested_action: Record in the pin file and firmware notes that M15 must be driven high; do not rely on leaving it unconstrained, since Vivado's default pull-down on unused pins (from memory, not checked) would fight R58. Alternatively, take U5 PG out of BOOT_RAILS_PG_3V3 on the next schematic revision.

findings.title: The ASICs are powered about 7 s before the Frontend is configured, with their clock and SPI inputs floating.
findings.what: On both FPGA-LDO A and the Option B LDO board, one RC (R1/C3) enables every ASIC regulator 15-22 ms after VIN_3V3 rises, whatever the FPGA is doing. The Frontend has PUDC_B strapped high, which turns off the FPGA's internal pull-ups during configuration, so the FPGA-driven ASIC clock (CLKH), SPI clock and SPI data lines float at the powered ASICs until configuration ends about 7 s later. Floating CMOS inputs can draw extra current and toggle at random. The files cannot settle whether this is safe, because the ASIC reset polarity and safe input states are unknown; an answer from the ASIC designer would settle it.
findings.where: FPGA-LDO A and Option B LDO board: R1 10k / C3 4.7 uF on /EN_ASIC_RAILS (U1 LT3582 SHDN, U2/U6/U8 LT3042, U9/U10 LT3094, U3/U4/U5/U7 TPS7A2015 EN); R2-R5, R16, R17, R18 10k pull-downs; R19 10k CHIP_RESET_SHARED pull-up to ASIC_DVDD. No pull on any board: BOARD1_CLK, BOARD3_CLK, BOARD1_SPI_CLK, BOARD3_SPI_CLK, STIM_CHIP1..4_SPI_DL/DR (Frontend U1 balls G16, V17, D10, V8, C11, G14, C14, C16, V7, V6, N17, N18; ASIC board CLKH, SPI_CLK, SPI_DINL/DINR). Frontend R25 470R PUDC_B to VCCO_1V5.
findings.evidence: exports/ldo_a/netlist.xml and exports/ldo_b_ldo/netlist.xml: /EN_ASIC_RAILS has 13 nodes (R1, C3, TP4, U1.8, U2-U10). The clock and SPI nets are 2-node nets on every LDO and router board, go straight to U1 balls on the Frontend and reach the ASIC pins with no resistor (exports/asic/netlist.xml). Enable delay t = 47 ms x ln(3.3/(3.3-V)): 15 ms at 0.9 V (TPS7A20 VEN(HI) max) and 22 ms at 1.24 V (LT3042 EN/UV rising, 1.18/1.24/1.32 V). Configuration: U12 hold 1.07 s (TPS3890 1.07 s per uF, C84 1 uF) plus 17,536,096 bits / 3 MHz = 5.85 s, about 7 s in total. inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/ASIC_REFERENCE.md rows U03/U05 and line 76: reset polarity and pad limits unknown.
findings.source: AMD UG470, 7 Series FPGAs Configuration User Guide: PUDC_B high disables I/O pull-ups during configuration (not opened, docs.amd.com returned 404; from memory). ASIC reference V1, rows U03/U05. Analog Devices LT3042 datasheet, EN/UV threshold row; TI TPS7A20 datasheet, VEN(HI) row; TI TPS3890 datasheet SLVSD65A, p.3.
findings.consequence: Powered ASICs with floating inputs may draw extra current and may clock random data into the configuration shift register, and whether CHIP_RESET held high and FE_RESET held low is a safe state is unknown. Boot also takes about 7 s unless the bitstream raises the configuration clock.
findings.suggested_action: Ask the ASIC designer for the reset polarity and the safe idle state of CLKH and SPI, then add pull-downs on the LDO board for the floating lines rather than setting PUDC_B low, whose weak pull-ups would fight the 10k pull-downs on STIM_EN, STIM_START and FE_RESET. Set BITSTREAM.CONFIG.CONFIGRATE as high as the U8 translator timing allows.

findings.title: The ASIC board thickness is unsettled: board file and fab job say 1.6 mm, fit and print models use 0.8 mm.
findings.what: The only ASIC board design and its PCBWay job file are 1.6 mm thick, but the project record says the ASIC board will be 0.8 mm, and the 11 Nov fit and print models draw it at 0.8 mm. findings.title: No file records the height of the ASIC dies and bond loops, which sit 1.5 mm under the next ASIC board.
findings.what: Each ASIC board carries two bare dies on its top side, joined to the board by fine bond wires that arch above the die (the bond loops). When ASIC boards stack, the next board's bare underside sits 1.5 mm above those dies, which is the mated height of the DF40 connector pair. No file records the die thickness, the bond-loop height or the height of any protective encapsulation (glob-top), and the fit models only use 0.5 mm boxes. The files cannot settle whether 1.5 mm is enough; die, loop and encapsulation heights from the ASIC designer or the bonding house would.
findings.where: ASIC board, top side: U01_BCD1 and U01_BCD2 pad area x 124.98-145.63, y 75.36-83.96. J4 (DF40C-80DP header) on top, J3 (DF40C-80DS receptacle) on the bottom. Affects two of the four ASIC boards in each option; in Option A, ASIC1 (under ASIC2) and ASIC4 (under ASIC3). The top board's dies are exposed.
findings.evidence: exports/asic/pads.csv: all 176 pads of U01_BCD1/U01_BCD2 on copper layer 1 (top); the only bottom-side part is J3 at y 69.47-72.55, so nothing hangs over the dies. Edge.Cuts in boards/asic/PCB.kicad_pcb: x 124.34-146.31, y 67.44-84.47. Hirose DF40 catalog text (scratch/system-mate-ldo-asic/df40_catalog.txt): 1.5 mm stacking height for DS receptacle with DP header. inputs/system/README_2026-11-11.md line 51: 'two dies are 0.5 mm boxes'; its Option A levels give 1.5 mm between ASIC1 and ASIC2 and between ASIC4 and ASIC3. ASIC3's dies have 4.58 mm up to ASIC1's underside because they lie past the LDO-A edge (y 110.34). inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference has no die thickness, loop height or glob-top value; U01 die and bonding revision listed as unknown.
findings.source: Hirose DF40 Series catalog, stacking height table, https://www.hirose.com/en/product/series/DF40; Engineering judgement for the clearance need.
findings.consequence: If die, loops and encapsulation together exceed about 1.4 mm, mating the next ASIC board can crush the bond wires of an irreplaceable ASIC.
findings.suggested_action: Get die thickness, loop height and encapsulation height from the ASIC designer or bonding house and record a maximum allowed height (for example 1.2 mm) in the ASIC board notes.

findings.already_known: Parts review V21 notes ILIM to GND and 'one fault takes down every ASIC' as accepted.
findings.title: ASIC rail regulators have no set current limit, so a fault shared by eight ASICs can draw 160-730 mA.
findings.what: All five LT3042/LT3094 regulators have their current-limit pin (ILIM) tied to ground, so only their internal limit applies (about 220-320 mA at low input voltage). The four TPS7A2015 regulators have no limit pin; their internal limit is 360-730 mA, folding back to about 160 mA into a hard short. Each regulator feeds all eight ASICs, which normally draw only 1.4-18 mA per rail in total. One resistor on ILIM would cap an LT3042 rail at about 50 mA, but that limit would still be shared by eight ASICs, and no file or datasheet shows that the present limits would fuse bond wires.
findings.where: FPGA-LDO Option A and Option B LDO board: U2, U6, U8, U9 pin 5 ILIM and U10 pin 6 ILIM on AGND (VDD_FE, REF_VDD, REF_VCM, VDD10, VSS10); U3, U4, U5, U7 TPS7A2015 (VDD_ADC, VDD_DRIVER, DVDD, VDD_CGEN).

findings.title: The Frontend FPGA can be configured only through the HDMI cable from a working HDMI Extension Board.
findings.what: JTAG is the four-wire test and programming port of the FPGA. On the Frontend, each JTAG net has just two pads, the FPGA ball and a contact on the Micro-HDMI connector, and the SPI flash can only be written through the FPGA. A first Frontend therefore needs a working HDMI Extension Board (USB-JTAG chip, switches set correctly, cable voltage check met) and a good cable; if any of these fails there is no fallback. A blank FT232H EEPROM mainly affects whether AMD's Vivado recognises the cable; open tools may still drive it (judgement, not checked).

findings.title: Clock and strobe edges may overshoot the 1.5 V ASIC rail by up to 0.4 V, and the ASIC pad limits are unknown.
findings.what: The FPGA drives the shared clock and strobe lanes with no series resistor, and the ASIC dies at the far ends are light loads, so the edges ring above the 1.5 V rail and below ground. A simple lossless model (no clamp diodes) puts the peak up to about 0.4 V over the rail at a 1.0 ns edge; about 0.6 V is reached only with a pessimistic 5 nH connector loop. That much overshoot is ordinary for unterminated CMOS, and at 0.4 V or less a silicon clamp diode conducts only a little, so current through the input protection on every edge is not shown. The real gap is that the ASIC's input absolute-maximum and clamp limits are not published; only the ASIC designer can say whether the pads tolerate this.

The 45 ohm for DRIVE 8 is the DS181 worst-case bound (VOL 25 % of VCCO at 8 mA), not a typical value; the SLOW-slew edge rate is not verified (no IBIS model).
findings.source: inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/ASIC_REFERENCE.md item U03; AMD DS181 Artix-7 Data Sheet v1.27.1, Table 4 (HR I/O overshoot VCCO + 0.55 V and undershoot -0.40 V for 100 % of the unit interval) and Table 8 (LVCMOS15 VOL), engineering judgement.
findings.consequence: If the ASIC pads tolerate only about 0.3 V outside their rail, the upper end of this overshoot could stress the input protection of dies that cannot be replaced, and the damage would be hard to trace.
findings.suggested_action: Ask the ASIC designer for the pad absolute-maximum and clamp ratings. Meanwhile use DRIVE 8 SLEW SLOW and probe CLKH at the far die's bond finger at first power-up with a probe of 1 GHz or more.

findings.title: On the ASIC board the clock and strobe lanes switch between the AGND and DGND planes with no tie between them.
findings.what: A fast signal's return current flows in the ground plane right under its trace. On the ASIC board the top-layer clock lanes run over the AGND (analog ground) plane and the bottom-layer lanes over the DGND (digital ground) plane, so at each through via the return current must jump between the two grounds. No capacitor or tie joins AGND and DGND on the board, so the return goes either through the rail decoupling capacitors and the capacitance between the stacked rail planes, or out through the J3/J4 ground contacts to the net tie NT1 on the LDO board. Either way, clock-edge current passes through the analog rails and AGND of a recording chip. How much noise this causes can only be judged by measurement.
findings.where: ASIC board: /CLKH vias at (142.14, 71.25) and (135.76, 84.11); 4 vias each on /STIM_CLK, /SPI_CLK, /SPI_LATCH and 6 on CHIP_RESET, all layers 1-10. F.Cu over In1 /AGND (L2), B.Cu over In8 /DGND (L9). LDO A: NT1 at (100.58, 121.0), 7.53 mm from J3/J4 at (99.78, 113.51).

AGND and DGND vias are separate nets. exports/asic/zones.csv: L2 /AGND 325.59 mm2, L3 VDD_FE, L4 REF_VDD, L5 REF_VCM, L6 VDD_DRIVER/VDD10, L7 VDD_ADC/VSS10, L8 DVDD, L9 /DGND 332.88 mm2. exports/asic/pads.csv: 16 placed capacitors go rail to AGND, only C7/C14 go DVDD to DGND; exports/asic/netlist.xml: none of the 50 schematic capacitors joins AGND and DGND. Estimated plane path: about 100 pF between VDD_ADC (L7) and DVDD (L8) across 0.1 mm (er 4.3, 263 mm2), then C7/C14 to DGND. NT1 exists only on ldo_a and ldo_b_ldo.
findings.source: Engineering judgement (return current follows the nearest reference plane; a change of reference plane needs a stitching path close to the via).
findings.consequence: Clock-edge noise in the ASIC analog ground and reference planes, and extra ringing on the clocks; this is outside the edge model of the other signal-integrity findings and only a measurement will show its size.
findings.suggested_action: When the second, not yet drawn ASIC board is laid out, keep clock lanes on the DGND-referenced layer end to end; on the existing board, measure AGND-DGND noise at J3/J4 while CLKH runs, before relying on it for recording.

findings.title: The XEM LVDS high level exceeds the Frontend's 1.5 V bank input limit only if VCCO_1V5 sags below 1.452 V.
findings.what: The Frontend receives the XEM's LVDS signals (low-voltage differential pairs) in banks powered at 1.5 V, while the XEM drives them from a 1.8 V bank. AMD allows this only if each input leg stays within the data-sheet recommended range, VCCO + 0.20 V. At the 1.50 V setpoint the highest leg voltage is 1.652 V against a 1.70 V limit, so there is 48 mV of margin and no violation. The limit is crossed only if VCCO_1V5 drops below 1.452 V (3.2 % low) while the XEM sits at both its maximum common-mode voltage and maximum swing.
findings.where: Frontend U1 P14/R15 (CABLE_CLK), M14/N14 (CABLE_CMDSYNC) in bank 14, B9/A9 (CABLE_SYNC) in bank 15, rail VCCO_1V5 from U4 (MPM3833C, R7 150k / R8 100k); driven from HDMI Extension Board XEM8310 bank 64 (HP, VIO1 1.8 V).

U4 setpoint 0.6 x (1 + 150k/100k) = 1.50 V; with VFB 591-609 mV the DC worst case is about 1.46 V, so a crossing also needs ripple or droop. Pins and standards: exports/frontend/pads.csv; inputs/frontend/V2_review_fixes/Frontend_V46_pins_V2.xdc (LVDS_25, DIFF_TERM FALSE on all six pins); inputs/hdmi/firmware_V34/fit_pins_V34.xdc (LVDS, bank 64, 1.8 V). The DS931 values come from a search summary (direct fetch failed), and the DS181 and MPM3833C values from third-party copies of the data sheets. Absolute rating is VCCO + 0.55 V (DS181 Table 4).

findings.suggested_action: No hardware change. Keep VCCO_1V5 at its 1.50 V setpoint with low ripple, and confirm it at bring-up.

findings.title: All eight ports share one enable from U700 power-good, so one FE_5V fault turns every stack off together.
findings.what: U700's power-good output (PG, a pin that goes low when the output voltage is out of range) drives PORT_ENABLE, which is the enable of all eight port power switches. PG goes low if FE_5V leaves its window for more than 120 us, or during U700 current limit or thermal shutdown. Every port then turns off at once and returns 1.5-2.5 ms after FE_5V recovers. Eight ports at their switch limits do not by themselves trip U700's current limit; realistic triggers are a sag of the +VDCIN input, thermal shutdown, or a load step beyond the regulation window.

findings.title: The ASIC rails come up in a fixed order, ±10 V last at about 0.25-0.5 s, and no required order is known.
findings.what: All ASIC regulators share one enable net that rises slowly through a resistor-capacitor (RC) delay, and each low-noise regulator's output follows a second RC on its SET pin, so the rails come up one after another. The 1.5 V TPS7A2015 rails start first (about 15 ms), the ±12 V boost/inverter rails are up by about 30 ms, VDD_FE and REF_VDD reach 90% at about 57 ms, and VDD10/VSS10 reach 90% at about 0.25 s and 99% at about 0.5 s. This low-voltage-first, ±10 V-last order is conventional and nothing in the files says it is wrong. The files cannot settle whether the ASIC accepts it, because no ASIC document states a required power-up order; only the ASIC designer can answer that.

findings.title: Returned CLK32MHz lines have no series resistor, so a strong ASIC driver could overshoot the FPGA input limit.
findings.what: Each ASIC drives its 32 MHz recording clock point-to-point to an FPGA clock pin with no series resistor, and the FPGA captures data on the falling edge. Overshoot is the voltage swinging above the supply; AMD limits how far above the 1.5 V bank supply an input may go and for how long. In a linear model of the far-chip (ASIC3) path the edge stays clean, but a strong, fast driver peaks near 2.5 V, about 1 V over the bank, beyond AMD's allowance, while a 30 ohm, 1 ns driver stays under about 1.7 V. The files cannot settle this because the ASIC output drive is unknown; a probe measurement at bring-up or the ASIC designer's driver data would.
